discovery: Optical lattice clocks: the magic-wavelength optical lattice clock and its realization at 10^-18 accuracy

nominees.name: Hidetoshi Katori
nominees.affiliation: University of Tokyo and RIKEN, Japan

nominees.name: Jun Ye
nominees.affiliation: JILA, NIST and University of Colorado Boulder, USA

motivation: Katori proposed in 2001, and then showed experimentally, that neutral atoms can be trapped in an optical lattice at a 'magic' wavelength. At that wavelength the light shifts of both clock states cancel. This went against the accepted view that trapping light necessarily perturbs the atoms it holds. It lets thousands of atoms be interrogated at once without Doppler or recoil effects, which gives optical clocks their high stability. Jun Ye developed the lattice clock into a quantum-limited instrument. He brought its systematic uncertainty and instability to the 10^-18 to 10^-19 level, resolved the gravitational redshift over a millimetre, and used many-body and spin-squeezing methods to improve it further. Together with the femtosecond frequency comb, lattice clocks now outperform the caesium standard by two orders of magnitude. They are driving the redefinition of the SI second, enabling relativistic geodesy and searches for new physics.
